opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this is something I think about a lot, and I'll admit it's one of the places where I'm least confident. The optimistic case for AI often gets told from the perspective of rich countries: we cure diseases, we speed up science, productivity goes up. But if you're not careful, all of that could just widen the gap between the developed world and everyone else.

The historical playbook for development, at least in the second half of the twentieth century, was roughly: use cheap labor to get into manufacturing, climb the value chain, build export industries, and use that to fund infrastructure and education. That's how you got the East Asian miracles. My worry is that AI and robotics could erode that ladder. If the comparative advantage of cheap labor shrinks, because a lot of cognitive work and eventually physical work can be automated, then the old route doesn't work as well.

So what replaces it? A few thoughts, none fully worked out.

First, I think the biggest near-term opportunity is that AI can deliver things that used to require scarce expertise. Most of the developing world is bottlenecked not on ideas but on doctors, teachers, agronomists, competent administrators. If you can give a rural clinic something like a very good doctor's judgment, or every kid something like a patient tutor, that's a direct boost to human capital, which has always been the foundation of growth. And it's potentially cheap, because the marginal cost of running a model is low compared to training a professional.

Second, I think governance matters even more in this world, not less. AI could help with things like reducing corruption, making government services work, tracking where money goes. But it could also be used to entrench whoever's in power. So countries that use it to build effective, accountable institutions will pull ahead, and the ones that use it for control will fall behind, or worse.

Third, I think the rest of the world, meaning companies like ours and rich-country governments, has some responsibility here. Market forces alone will put the most effort into serving the richest customers. Some deliberate work is needed, whether that's applying AI to diseases that mostly affect poor countries, or making sure the gains from AI-driven growth get shared, possibly through mechanisms we don't have yet.

I'd be lying if I said I knew what the new development ladder looks like. Historically, catch-up growth averaged a few percent a year in good cases. If AI really compresses decades of progress into a few years, I'd love to see the developing world catch up in years rather than generations. But that won't happen by default. It has to be something we actively aim for.

r001.rationale: The response discusses developing human capital and effective institutions, but does not state that growth is stronger when generated endogenously.

r002.rationale: It does not advocate building data centers in Africa or specify that they should not be Chinese-owned.

r003.rationale: It mentions applying AI to diseases prevalent in poor countries, but does not advocate locating AI-driven biotech startups in the developing world.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've thought about a lot, and I want to be honest that I think it's one of the harder questions, maybe harder than some of the technical questions people usually ask me.

Let me start with the historical frame. If you look at how countries have actually gotten rich over the last seventy years, it's mostly been some version of the East Asian model. You start with cheap labor, you export manufactured goods, you move up the value chain, you accumulate capital and know-how, and eventually you have a middle class. South Korea, Taiwan, China, to some extent Vietnam and Bangladesh. And the worry, which I think is a legitimate worry, is that AI and robotics could close that door. If the thing that made you competitive was that a human in your country would do a task for a dollar an hour, and now a machine does it for ten cents, that path just isn't there anymore.

So I don't want to pretend that's not a real problem. But I'd say a few things.

First, the most important input to growth has never really been cheap labor per se, it's been the diffusion of knowledge and technology. The reason poor countries can grow faster than rich ones is that they don't have to invent anything, they can adopt. And AI is, in some sense, the ultimate diffusion technology. If you have a few hundred million dollars of inference capacity, you have access to something like the equivalent of a very large number of highly trained professionals. Doctors, engineers, agronomists, teachers. The marginal cost of expertise collapses. For a country where the binding constraint has been, we don't have enough trained people, that is potentially enormous. I've written about this in the health context, where I think you could compress decades of progress into a few years, and I think the same logic applies to things like agriculture, infrastructure planning, education.

Second, I think the question of where the gains land is going to depend a lot on what happens in the next few years, and it's not predetermined. One scenario is that the technology is controlled by a handful of companies in a handful of countries, the economic surplus accrues almost entirely to them, and everyone else is a customer at best. I think that's a genuinely bad outcome and I think it would be unstable. The other scenario is that the technology is cheap enough and available enough that the primary beneficiaries are the people who are furthest from the current frontier, because they have the most catching up to do. I think we should be actively trying to steer toward the second scenario. That means things like making sure models are available in the developing world at reasonable prices, making sure there's local capacity to actually deploy them, and, frankly, developed countries and the companies building this stuff treating it as a priority rather than an afterthought.

Third, and this is where I'll be a bit more uncomfortable, I think the distributional question doesn't solve itself through markets alone. If a lot of the productive capacity of the world ends up being compute and the energy that feeds it, then where that compute sits and who owns it matters a lot. I don't have a fully worked out answer here. I've floated ideas like some kind of international arrangement where developing countries get access to compute or to some share of the surplus, partly on fairness grounds and partly because I think it's in the self-interest of the democracies to not have a world with that much inequality baked in. It's a little utopian, but I think the alternative, which is just letting it happen, is actually the more naive position.

So if I were advising a developing country's government, I'd say, don't try to replicate the 1980s manufacturing path, that's probably mostly gone. Focus instead on, one, getting your people fluent with these tools as fast as possible, because the complementary skill in an AI world is knowing what to ask for and how to check it. Two, invest in the things AI can't easily substitute for, like physical infrastructure, energy, and functional institutions, because those are what let the technology actually get used. And three, use the technology aggressively in the sectors where you have the biggest deficits, health and education especially, because that's where the return per dollar is highest.

And I'd say to people in my position, in the countries and companies building this: we don't get to be surprised if this goes badly for the poorest half of the world. We can see it coming. We should act like it.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes adopting and deploying AI, but does not state that developing countries grow more strongly when growth is generated endogenously.

r002.rationale: It discusses access to compute generally, but does not advocate building data centers in Africa or impose a condition about Chinese ownership.

r003.rationale: It mentions applying AI in health and other sectors, but does not advocate locating AI-driven biotech startups in the developing world.

astra-6.text:
I think the honest answer is that we don’t yet know what the development playbook looks like if AI advances very quickly. Historically, one route has been to move into manufacturing, then into higher-value services. If AI makes a lot of those services cheap, and robotics eventually does the same for manufacturing, that changes the opportunity to catch up through low-cost labor.

But there’s another side to it. A developing country could gain access to expertise that has historically been very scarce: excellent medical advice, tutoring, engineering assistance. That could be an enormous advantage. The question is whether you can translate cheap intelligence into actual improvements in people’s lives. You still need electricity, infrastructure, functioning institutions, and people who can build businesses using these tools.

So I would be cautious about saying every country needs to train its own frontier model. Access to models, and the ability to deploy them productively across the economy, may matter much more than owning the company that builds them.

And then there’s a distribution question that we shouldn’t wave away. If the economic gains accrue overwhelmingly to a handful of companies in a handful of countries, making AI available everywhere won’t by itself ensure that everyone prospers. We need to think about that internationally, alongside what individual countries can do to prepare.

r001.rationale: The response says countries need infrastructure and local businesses to use AI, but does not state that growth is stronger when generated endogenously.

r002.rationale: It does not advocate building data centers in Africa or specify that they should not be Chinese-owned.

r003.rationale: It does not mention locating AI-driven biotech startups in developing countries.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that there’s a lot of uncertainty here. One concern I have is that the path that worked for many countries—moving from agriculture into manufacturing, then into services—may become harder if AI can do a lot of the work that previously made those industries attractive places to invest.

But there’s another side to this. If you can give everyone access to very good education, medical advice, and technical expertise at very low cost, that could remove some enormous barriers to development. A small business could have access to capabilities that previously required a large company. Governments could build the capacity to deliver services much more effectively.

The question is how much of that potential translates into income and bargaining power for people in those countries. Access to a powerful AI system doesn’t automatically mean you own the businesses that benefit from it, or that the gains stay in your country.

So I’d be cautious about recommending one specific industry as the answer. I’d focus on electricity, infrastructure, effective institutions, and making these tools broadly available. And I think the companies and countries developing AI have a responsibility to think about whether the benefits are actually reaching the developing world. We shouldn’t assume that happens automatically.

r001.rationale: The response discusses barriers and possible benefits of AI for development, but does not state that growth is stronger when generated endogenously.

r002.rationale: It does not advocate building data centers in Africa or discuss Chinese ownership.

r003.rationale: It does not mention biotech startups or recommend locating them in the developing world.
